_comment: The turn-outcome rule, as a table both languages must satisfy.
The rule is implemented twice on purpose and neither copy can go: the server
derives outcome for the whole session (internal/chat/turns.go deriveTurnOutcome)
because the timeline rail must describe turns the paginated client store does
not hold, and the client derives the IN-FLIGHT turn's outcome
(static-src/turns.ts deriveOutcome) because no fetched summary can know a turn
that is still streaming.
This file is the contract between them. It is read by TestTurnOutcomeContract
(Go) and by turns.node.test.ts (TypeScript). Changing the rule in one language
fails the other language's test, which is the only mechanism keeping the two
in agreement — there is no code generation for behaviour.
`body` lists the turn's non-trigger messages. `refusal` true means the message
carries a refusal marker; `event` names an inline event's kind. `is_live` is
the caller's 'this is the last turn and the session is thinking' flag.
THE WRITER AND THE READER ARE ONE MECHANISM, so the tail clause below only
holds because persistOutcomeMarker skips a carrier for one shape alone: a turn
NO row on disk represents. It used to omit the carrier for a clean prompted
empty turn — the reader's default already said `completed`, so the row looked
redundant — which made a legitimately clean empty turn byte-identical on disk
to one a restart killed. Now a close whose turn a persisted TRIGGER represents
always leaves the outcome on a ROW — the marker, or the cancel row that is
already one — so a body carrying no assistant message and no settled outcome
means NOTHING closed the turn, and `unknown` is a fact rather than a guess.
Restore that skip and the two `unknown` rows below become unreachable.
That one skip does not reach them. An ENGINE-OPENED turn (a KAS auto-wake, a
workflow step) that carried nothing persists NO carrier: nothing else stands
for it, so the marker would BE the whole turn and it opens a headerless card
holding nothing (persistsEmptyCarrier). A turn SPLIT at a compaction point is
exempt — it has a sealed assistant row already, and segmentMessage stamps no
outcome, so there the marker is the only carrier the turn's verdict and footer
have. Both `unknown` rows describe a turn WITH a user row, which a prompted
close still carries a marker for. For a turn that persists NOTHING the END is
a separate axis: a KAS auto-wake still announces its end (announcesEmptyEnd)
where a step's belongs to its run, and an announcement persists nothing, so
it reaches neither projection.
The predicate is 'no assistant message', not 'an empty body', and that is what
protects every turn already on disk: this chat file only ever gained an
assistant message at finalize, so a legacy turn carries one and still reads
`completed` — the row named for that carve-out is what stops a later reader
widening the clause.
ACCEPTED RESIDUAL, stated rather than fixed: a restart-killed turn whose
mid-turn compaction SEALED a segment does have an assistant message on disk
(SealTurnSegment -> segmentMessage), and that segment carries no outcome by
construction, so such a turn still reads `completed`. Stamping an outcome on a
segment would put two carriers in one turn and break the exactly-one-carrier
invariant.

cases.name: a clean finished turn
a turn nothing closed reads unknown, not completed
_comment: The reported population: a prompt refused after its user row landed, a cancel
during the spawn/prime/MCP window, and a process death mid-turn all persist the
user row and nothing else. This row used to want `completed`, which reported
every one of them as a turn that answered.

cases.name: a turn nothing closed YET is still running, not unknown
_comment: The live half, and why the clause sits below the isLive one: the carrier arrives
at finalize, so an in-flight turn legitimately has none and must not be reported
as an end nobody could read.

cases.name: a legacy turn with an assistant message and no outcome still completed
_comment: THE CARVE-OUT, and the row that stops a later reader widening the clause to
'an empty carrier'. Measured over the live records: 8 of the 14 carrier-less
turns are richly-answered legacy turns, two of them 185 and 265 blocks. Reading
those as failures would be a regression, not a fix.

a refusal fails the turn
a blocked infra-safety write fails the turn
a failed compaction fails the turn
a cancel interrupts the turn
an interrupt interrupts the turn
a refusal beats the running flag
an interrupt beats the running flag
failed beats interrupted when a turn carries both
failed beats interrupted regardless of order
a model switch is not an outcome
a successful compaction is not a FAILURE
_comment: This row's real property is that a compaction does not make a turn failed, and
that is unchanged. It wanted `completed` while an absent carrier defaulted that
way; a body holding one event row and no assistant message is now a turn nothing
closed, so it wants `unknown`. Either way the assertion worth having is that it
is not `failed`.

a durable outcome beats the running flag
a cancelled turn says cancelled, not interrupted
a refusal recorded on the wire says refused
an unmapped stop reason says unknown rather than failed
a later settled outcome supersedes a fragment's unknown
a fragment inside a live turn reads as running
an interrupt beats a fragment's unknown
a truncated turn still completed

_segmentation_comment: The BOUNDARY rule, and reviewers caught it wrong in both directions, so it is
pinned rather than described. A user message opens a turn; so does the first
persisted message of a turn with NO user trigger, which is derivable because a
turn's SETTLED-outcome-bearing message closes it.
Too narrow (only an empty turn's marker opens one) puts a non-empty
agent-initiated turn's outcome in the PREVIOUS turn's body, which can flip a
completed turn to failed on reload. Too broad (any non-user message opens one)
splits a prompted empty turn that has a user message to attach to.
An outcome of `unknown` does NOT close: it marks a fragment whose end never
arrived (a displaced wire turn's persist), and transcripts persisted before
the internal-tool suppression carry one per fresh session between the user
message and the real reply. Closing on it split that turn in two — a phantom
'Agent-initiated turn' holding the actual answer, and a rail one turn long.
THIS PARAGRAPH IS THE ONE OWNER OF THE TWO OPENING RULES, and neither
projection twin restates them. A PROMPT opens a turn, and a STEER — a user row
carrying `user_kind: steer` — joins the turn already running, because the reader
was correcting work in flight rather than asking for more. A message whose EVERY
block is workflow-step content opens nothing, because the transcript draws none
of it: `messages-blocks.ts` placeBlock DROPS a block whose subtask id parses as
`wf:<workflowId>:<nodePath>`, so a card opened for such a message renders an
empty body. One block of the agent's own prose, one malformed `wf:` id (which
still renders, as a delegate box) is drawn, so such a message keeps its card,
and so does a blockless message for as long as it carries content. A message
carrying NOTHING — no content, no reasoning, no blocks, no tool calls, no plan,
no refusal, no outcome — opens nothing, because there is nothing yet to draw:
it is what the live wire's first frame for a turn looks like.
A FRAGMENT IS A CORRELATION, NOT THE CAUSE. Keying either rule on a
`turn_outcome` of `unknown` reaches some of the same messages and does so for
the wrong reason: what stops a card is that the message renders nothing, which a
fragment neither implies nor is implied by — a settled step message renders
nothing, and a fragment carrying the agent's own prose renders.
Measured 2026-09-08 and stated as DELTAS, because every absolute total here
rots as the live volume grows: the step rule removes 5 rail turns and the
steer rule a further 13, each chat's steer-rule move equalling its own count
of persisted steer rows.
`messages` is the flat persisted list. `want` is one entry per expected turn:
its opening message id, whether it has a user trigger, and its outcome.
`blocks` lists one subtask id per block; absent means the message carries no
blocks at all. `empty` suppresses the content every other row carries, which is
the only way to stage a message that carries nothing.

segmentation.name: a prompted non-empty turn is one segment
a displaced boot fragment does not split its prompt's turn
a lone fragment keeps its unknown outcome
a prompted EMPTY turn is not split off from its own prompt
a non-empty agent-initiated turn's outcome does not land on the previous turn
an EMPTY agent-initiated turn is its own turn and appears in the index
an EMPTY agent-initiated COMPLETED turn is its own turn and appears in the index
_comment: `completed` is the derivation's default, which is why the marker is skipped
for a PROMPTED empty turn: its user message already represents it. The skip is
therefore semantic (a persisted trigger already represents this turn), never
`outcome == completed`.
This row is a READER rule and it is NOT the writer's mirror. The writer no
longer mints this exact shape for a fresh turn: an ENGINE-OPENED turn that
left no row of its own persists no marker either, deliberately, because a
marker with nothing beside it IS the whole turn and opens a headerless card
holding nothing. What still reaches the reader here is a turn already on disk
from before that ruling, and a CANCELLED empty engine turn, whose EventCancelled
row is appended ahead of the skip and carries the outcome. So do not narrow the
reader on the strength of the writer's narrowing — the rows it must keep
projecting outlive it.

segmentation.name: an interrupt divider stays with the turn it describes
two agent-initiated turns in a row are two turns
a message whose every block is workflow-step content opens no turn
a message mixing step blocks with its own prose still opens a turn
an assistant message with no blocks still opens a turn
an assistant message carrying nothing opens no turn
_comment: The row above with its content taken away, which is the only difference between
the two. It is the shape the live wire produces first: `ensureTurnStarted`
announces a message id and a role before any content frame, so a turn opened
here renders a card with nothing in it until the reader reloads.

segmentation.name: a malformed step subtask id still opens a turn
a settled reply after step content opens its own turn
_comment: THE DISCRIMINATOR: every other row here answers the same way whether the rule
keys on step content or on a fragment, and this one does not. The step message
stays in the prompt's turn and `a3`, the settled reply, opens one of its own —
so the turn is RELOCATED rather than suppressed, and that is the ACCEPTED
answer rather than an oversight.
Measured 2026-09-08: this rule removes 5 rail turns and the steer rule a
further 13. The turns a segment-closing rule would ALSO suppress — 86, of
which 81 carry renderable content — are agent-initiated turns opened by
settled assistant messages carrying real prose: a separate mechanism, out of
scope for this rule, and suppressing them would cost real work its own card.

segmentation.name: a legacy transcript with no durable outcomes segments as it always did
a steer joins the turn already running
two steers in one turn are still one turn
a steer after a settled close joins the closed turn and opens nothing
a steer opening the window gets a headerless turn
_comment: THE ACCEPTED RENDERING, pinned so a later reader does not 'fix' it into a
trigger. The label says agent-initiated for a row the reader typed, because
`agent_initiated` really means 'this turn has no PROMPT to head it' and a steer
is not a prompt. It is unreachable for the rail, which projects the whole
session, and reachable only for the client's paginated window when the first
page starts mid-turn — the same shape a page opening on an assistant message
already produces. Fixing it means renaming the `agent_initiated` wire field,
which is a separate change.
